players.product: Jenbacher gas engines and gensets (Type 6 / J624 platform; containerized 5 MW units and multi-pack configurations) for behind-the-meter prime and backup power at AI data centers; Jenbacher power-solutions gensets (utility, peaker, biogas); Waukesha gas compression engines; lifecycle services

quarterly_data.signal: First earnings call as a listed company. Q2 2026 revenue $938 million, up 42% year-over-year (equipment $569 million, +61%; services $368 million, +21%); H1 2026 revenue $1.6 billion, up 39%. Adjusted EBITDA $172 million, up 20%; adjusted segment EBITDA $188 million, up 24%, at a 20% segment margin. CFO Dennis Schulze: the EBITDA margin is 'notably below prior year', driven by the natural mix shift toward equipment, a higher share of containerized solutions in product scope, and front-loaded investments and ramp-up costs for the capacity expansion; the margin is in line with Q1 2026 and ahead of the planned path for the year. Free cash flow $205 million, up 352%; customer down payments keep equipment manufacturing cash positive from order to commissioning.
quarterly_data.figure: Q2 revenue $938 million (+42% YoY); equipment $569 million (+61%); services $368 million (+21%); adjusted EBITDA $172 million (+20%); free cash flow $205 million (+352%)

quarterly_data.signal: Q2 2026 equipment revenue by business line: data center revenue nearly doubled to $232 million (CFO Dennis Schulze: Q1 2026 was $107 million), power solutions $274 million, compression $63 million. Equipment adjusted segment EBITDA margin 14% versus 19% a year earlier, reflecting self-funded growth investments and increased order scope; CFO: 'This expanded scope for the early data center products was priced with a lower average margin than our core business.' The equipment margin improved from 'slightly ahead of 7%' in Q1 to 14%, and the CFO expects equipment segment margins to reach the high teens in Q4 on operating leverage and backlog pricing dynamics, an upturn 'mainly driven by the data center revenues now flowing through the funnel'.
quarterly_data.figure: data center revenue $232 million (Q1 2026: $107 million); power solutions $274 million; compression $63 million; equipment segment margin 14% (prior-year quarter 19%)

quarterly_data.signal: Record Q2 equipment order intake of $2.3 billion, up 316% year-over-year: data center close to $1.5 billion, power solutions $546 million, compression $281 million, each business line growing strongly. CFO Dennis Schulze: H1 order intake of $3.9 billion already exceeds the entire year of 2025; equipment book-to-bill 4.4 for the first six months. CEO Olaf Berlien: LTM equipment order intake $6.6 billion versus $3.9 billion in 2025. Equipment order backlog a record $6.6 billion at June 30, 2026, up 279% year-over-year and up 83% in H1 from $3.6 billion at end-2025, with sequential growth in every quarter. CEO: follow-on orders came from hyperscaler customers and colocation providers executing phased data center build-outs; 'no single customer represents an outsized share of our order book'; he expects the order backlog at year-end to be higher than today.
quarterly_data.figure: Q2 order intake $2.3 billion (+316% YoY); data center close to $1.5 billion; power solutions $546 million; compression $281 million; backlog $6.6 billion (+279% YoY, +83% in H1); H1 book-to-bill 4.4

quarterly_data.signal: CFO Dennis Schulze: combining the equipment order backlog with slot reservations, INNIO has 'more than 15 GW of committed business as of Q2 2026', more than four times the power delivered over the last 12 months. Slot reservations are production slot commitments that are non-tradable and typically carry a non-refundable down payment (Martin Widner, head of global sales for data centers and power solutions: each is dedicated to a single project). Approximately 64% of the more than 15 GW relates to behind-the-meter data center solutions, and within data center around 94% is prime power. Widner: the 6% backup power is where diesel engines were replaced with gas engines because at very large data center hubs diesel NOx emissions would be too high (one hyperscaler chose gas engines); INNIO could win more diesel-to-gas backup orders but, given capacity, looks 'very detailed' at how much to give to prime versus backup power. The CFO says the expected service intensity of this backlog is substantially above the installed-base average because data center customers run the engines as their primary power source. Management will not split the 15 GW between backlog and slot reservations.
quarterly_data.figure: more than 15 GW committed (backlog plus slot reservations); ~64% behind-the-meter data center; ~94% of data center prime power, 6% backup

quarterly_data.signal: FY2026 guidance initiated (CFO Dennis Schulze): revenue $3.8 billion-$3.9 billion, growth of approximately 46% at the midpoint versus 2025, with the mix shifting further to equipment at around 65% of revenue and revenue growth expected to accelerate in H2; adjusted EBITDA $720 million-$740 million, an increase of 33% (roughly one-third) versus $549 million in 2025, at a group margin of approximately 19%. The fourth quarter is expected to be stronger than the third on shipment cadence against the backlog and the ramp-up of added capacity; equipment segment adjusted EBITDA margin expected to reach an exit rate in the high teens by year-end.
quarterly_data.figure: FY2026 revenue $3.8 billion-$3.9 billion (~46% growth at midpoint); adjusted EBITDA $720 million-$740 million (+33%); group margin ~19%; equipment ~65% of revenue

quarterly_data.signal: Capacity sold out (management): CEO Olaf Berlien: 'We are more or less sold out for 26, 27'; delivery times being discussed today are 2029 and 2030, customers with many projects are talking about 2030 and 2031, and the 1.1 GW order announced on the call delivers until 2031. Martin Widner (head of global sales for data centers and power solutions): 'the slot reservation reaches out now till 2030'; '2027 is completely sold out, so there are no further slots to be freed up for 2027', with slots now being freed for 2028 and, with the further Waukesha ramp-up, 2029 and 2030; 'We still have many requests for projects which we are not able to fulfill because of capacity'; 'capacity constraint, but not market constraint.' CFO Dennis Schulze: demand 'has recently been exceeding our ability to take orders'; INNIO is deliberately not selling the whole planned capacity curve yet and frees up slots over time as the ramp-up proves on time and in spec.
quarterly_data.figure: 2027 completely sold out; slot reservations reach out to 2030

quarterly_data.signal: Capacity expansion (CFO Dennis Schulze): INNIO plans to roughly double output in the coming years and approximately triple total production capacity from 3.5 GW per year in 2025 to roughly 10 GW per year by 2030; GW delivered in Q2 were already 1.3x the prior year, and output will be ahead of 3.5 GW this year. The scale-up goes first to seven GW based on the Jenbach site, then up to 10 GW with the further ramp-up in Waukesha from 2028 onwards; both projects are on track and the 10 GW level is reviewed on an ongoing basis. The expansion is brownfield (debottlenecking existing facilities) and financed from operating cash flow: a new assembly line plus debottlenecking at the Jenbach campus in Austria for data center products; additional machining capacity including a new site in Hall near Jenbach; new U.S. sites in Trenton, New Jersey and Waller, Texas dedicated to containerization and packaging, close to key suppliers and customers; expanded machining and assembly in Waukesha, Wisconsin and Welland, Ontario. As capacity comes online INNIO expects to release incremental production slots that can convert into additional order intake.
quarterly_data.figure: 3.5 GW per year (2025) to roughly 10 GW per year by 2030; Q2 GW delivered 1.3x prior year

quarterly_data.signal: Large orders (management): CEO Olaf Berlien: the Q2 highlight was a 1.1 GW order from a megascale data center customer (not named), one of the largest orders in INNIO's history, with more than 200 Jenbacher J624 engines expected to provide behind-the-meter prime power and delivery until 2031. Martin Widner: the order is 'even below 30%' of the quarter's data center order intake; part of it is containerized (more scope) and part is for a powerhouse installation (less scope). CFO Dennis Schulze: 'Size of 1.1 GW is not the exception, it's now, I would say, common.' CEO: 'we announced the Greco [as transcribed; Aggreko] one was 1.25 GW. It's a little bit longer run project'; 'we are working with Greco, a long-term contract delivering engines Type four, Type six. There are many of these coming up.'
quarterly_data.figure: 1.1 GW order; more than 200 J624 engines; below 30% of Q2 data center order intake; 1.25 GW long-term contract

quarterly_data.signal: Demand and customers (management): CEO Olaf Berlien: 'There is no decline or weaknesses in the pipeline', strength is expected in H2, and additional customers are entering the top customer profile; of the 'six or seven big hyperscalers, they are all our customers'; 'we do not have one single cancellation today in smaller project as well as in big projects', citing diligence on project financing and customers. Martin Widner: demand for INNIO's product 'is as high as ever', with projects in 2029, 2030 and 2031 and a pipeline developed with Energy-as-a-Service and rental companies for different hyperscalers 'going into permits already into plans for 2031, 2032'; customer projects are on time with no big construction or permitting delays so far; the containerized solution needs little on-site EPC capability, an advantage while U.S. EPC capacity is constrained. CEO: behind-the-meter gas engines 'are not the bridge solution, but are here to stay' (citing a BloombergNEF analysis that gas engines can offer the lowest levelized cost of energy among behind-the-meter technologies), and the Ratepayer Protection Pledge signed by nearly all utilities and several colocation companies is 'a sign of growing support for behind-the-meter power'. Management says the Jenbacher T6 platform (incl. J624) offers industry-leading power density, fast response times and higher rotational inertia for dynamic AI data center loads, with a modular design that accelerates time to power.
quarterly_data.figure: no cancellations; all six or seven big hyperscalers are customers (CEO)

quarterly_data.signal: Markets beyond data centers (management): CEO Olaf Berlien: power solutions, 'our core business', is growing as coal-fired generation retires and renewable penetration rises, supported by continued demand for peaker plants that help maintain grid stability, with continued momentum in biogas solutions, especially in Germany, and growing potential in the U.S.; in Germany the government agreed that 9 GW is coming to the market, with auction deliveries in 2029, 2030 and 2031, plus another 2 GW in an auction for 2027. Martin Widner: big auctions in Brazil and auctions coming in Argentina; 'I'm even, to be honest, a bit concerned about the capacity we have because there are so many other markets coming up.'
quarterly_data.figure: Germany: 9 GW coming to market, plus 2 GW auction for 2027 (CEO)

quarterly_data.signal: Pricing (management): CEO Olaf Berlien: 'the pricing trend is clearly still strong'; 'If the demand is high and delivery is limited, you are always in a good position to do something on prices. I do not see any signals going down on price trend.' CFO Dennis Schulze: pricing on recent order bookings shows a positive margin trend compared with the historical average ('This is not growth at any price'), new orders generally carry accretive pricing and higher service intensity than past business, and as the backlog grows the embedded profitability is expected to grow with it.

Company profile (CEO Olaf Berlien): INNIO delivers decentralized power solutions for critical infrastructure and the AI industry under the Jenbacher (power generation) and Waukesha (gas compression) brands; 2025 revenue $2.6 billion and adjusted EBITDA $549 million. Two segments: Equipment (52% of 2025 revenue; business lines data center, power solutions and compression) and Services (48%). Data center was 59% and power solutions 35% of 2025 equipment order intake. Installed base approximately 44 GW globally as of 2025; more than 5,000 employees; business in 100 countries.
quarterly_data.figure: 2025 revenue $2.6 billion; adjusted EBITDA $549 million; installed base ~44 GW; data center 59% of 2025 equipment order intake; Equipment 52% / Services 48% of 2025 revenue

quarterly_data.signal: Services (CFO Dennis Schulze): Q2 services adjusted segment EBITDA margin 30% (H1 31%), helped by a margin-accretive parts-versus-labor mix that largely offset growth investments in parts capacity and the service force; CEO Olaf Berlien: LTM service revenue $1.4 billion at a 30% adjusted segment EBITDA margin. The Waukesha business line is more transactional and parts-driven; Q2 parts strength may partly reflect a cut-off tailwind, with no slowdown seen so far. The data center fleet is not yet a service driver: its main service events are minor and major overhauls after 30K and 60K operating hours, which the CFO says start hitting the P&L about four years out, with the real service contribution 'from the early 2030s onwards'; he sees confidence to 'deliver or even over-deliver' on the service plan. Equipment adjusted EBITDA generally carries 2.5x lifecycle services adjusted EBITDA, a relationship the CFO expects to deliver or improve. INNIO is building the scale of its North American services offering.
quarterly_data.figure: LTM service revenue $1.4 billion (30% margin); H1 services margin 31%; equipment EBITDA carries 2.5x lifecycle services EBITDA
